title: Maple-Cured Salmon Plank
shortDescription: Cedar-planked salmon with maple glaze for ten on the grill
subtitle: Cedar-planked salmon with maple glaze for ten on the grill
description: Salmon fillets get a quick maple-brine, then grill on cedar planks until edges caramelize and centers stay moist. Flake onto platters with lemon-dill yogurt and roasted asparagus.

steps.title: Gather ingredients and equipment
steps.instruction: Line up every ingredient for Maple-Cured Salmon Plank in the order you will cook — measure spices into ramekins, trim proteins on a dedicated board, and set tongs, thermometers, and hotel pans within arm's reach before any heat goes on.

steps.title: Preheat ovens and surfaces
steps.instruction: Preheat ovens, griddles, or grills to recipe temp before the crew arrives — cold equipment extends cook time and dries out batch salmon. Confirm burners ignite evenly and sheet pans are greased or lined.

steps.title: Brine the salmon
steps.instruction: Dissolve salt in cold water with maple syrup. Submerge salmon 30–60 minutes, then pat completely dry. Work in batches if the pan or grill crowding steams food instead of browning — rookies should watch for pale surfaces and adjust heat early.

steps.title: Soak cedar planks
steps.instruction: Submerge planks in water at least 1 hour so they smolder instead of catching fire on the grill. Cook until char marks are visible and the thickest piece reads 165°F on an instant-read thermometer. Work in batches if the pan or grill crowding steams food instead of browning — rookies should watch for pale surfaces and adjust heat early.

steps.title: Prep glaze and sauce
steps.instruction: Whisk maple syrup, brown sugar, Dijon, and soy for glaze. Mix yogurt, dill, lemon zest, and juice for sauce. Refrigerate until service.

steps.title: Grill on planks
steps.instruction: Heat grill to medium-high, about 400°F. Place salmon on planks, close lid, and grill 12–15 minutes until centers reach 125°F for medium or 140°F for well-done. Target oven/smoker temperature: 400°F.

steps.title: Verify safe internal temps
steps.instruction: Spot-check the thickest pieces with an instant-read thermometer — target 165°F. If any piece reads low, return it to heat immediately rather than holding under temp on the line.

steps.title: Hold for call interruptions
steps.instruction: If tones drop mid-service, cover finished food and hold at 140°F in a warm cabinet or 200°F oven — never leave proteins below 140°F for more than 30 minutes cumulative. Note the hold time on the pan with a grease pencil.

steps.title: Portion and open the line
steps.instruction: Portion Maple-Cured Salmon Plank onto sheet trays or hotel pans for family-style service. Stack plates, forks, and napkins at the end of the line so late-arriving crew can self-serve without bottlenecking the cook.

steps.title: Scale for larger halls
steps.instruction: When cooking for more than 8 firefighters, split into two pans halfway through so the bottom layer does not overcook while the top waits — duplicate mise en place if you double batches.

steps.title: Glaze and platter
steps.instruction: Brush glaze in final 6 minutes. Rest salmon 5 minutes, flake or portion onto platters with yogurt sauce and grilled asparagus. Cook until char marks are visible and the thickest piece reads 165°F on an instant-read thermometer. Keep a backup tray at 200°F for firefighters returning from a call — never serve picked-over pans to late crew.

proTips: Keep a spray bottle near the grill—planks can flare if glaze drips.
Offer capers for crew who want a bagel-and-lox vibe without the bagels.
Save plank trim for smoking wood chips on the next BBQ night.
tonightSpread: Planked salmon with dill yogurt, grilled asparagus, and lemon wedges.
Wild rice pilaf for a plate that feels complete without heavy starches.
leftovers: Flake cold salmon into salads with the yogurt sauce as dressing.
Make salmon cakes with panko and egg for a fast lunch shift.
whyCrewsLikeIt: Salmon night upgrades the hall menu without feeling fussy. Plank grilling keeps fish off direct flame, reduces sticking, and delivers real smoke aroma—even on a gas grill behind the station.
mealPrepNotes: Brine fillets up to 4 hours ahead. Soak cedar planks at least 1 hour. Pat salmon dry before grilling so maple glaze caramelizes instead of steaming off.
